faq.a: Acute hemolysis may be offset by dehydration; repeat Hb after rehydration to reveal true anemia.
faq.q: Why can a patient with severe malaria have normal Hb on admission?

faq.a: Yes, chronic intestinal blood loss from hookworm leads to iron‑deficiency anemia.
Short‑term iron is acceptable; avoid large bolus in active severe infection where bacteria may use iron.
faq.q: Is it safe to give iron to a patient with infection?

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman in labour has Hb 9 g/dL – what immediate steps do you take? — Assess hemodynamics, give IV iron if time permits, arrange cross‑matched blood, monitor for postpartum hemorrhage.

A child from a malaria‑endemic area presents with pallor and Hb 6 g/dL – how do you differentiate iron deficiency from malaria‑related anemia? — Perform malaria smear, check ferritin; treat malaria first, then give iron if ferritin low.

You receive a CBC showing Hb 19 g/dL in a 45‑year‑old smoker living at 1500 m altitude – what is your differential? — Secondary polycythemia from chronic hypoxia, primary polycythemia vera; obtain EPO level and consider phlebotomy.
A patient on antiretroviral therapy has Hb 10 g/dL, MCV 105 fL – what is the likely cause and management? — Zidovudine‑induced macrocytic anemia; switch to alternative ART and give folic acid.

During a blood transfusion a patient develops fever and chills – what does this indicate about Hb management? — Possible transfusion reaction; stop transfusion, treat reaction, reassess need for further blood.

In a rural clinic without a CBC, a patient has signs of anemia – what bedside investigations can you use? — Look for conjunctival pallor, nail bed pallor, tachycardia; estimate severity and decide on empirical iron or referral.

A patient with known sickle‑cell disease presents with severe pain and Hb 7 g/dL – what are the priorities? — Pain control, hydration, oxygen, consider exchange transfusion if Hb falls rapidly or signs of stroke.
Why is phlebotomy contraindicated in a dehydrated patient with high Hb? — Phlebotomy would worsen hypovolemia; first correct dehydration, then reassess Hb.
ai.title: Hemoglobin Concentration
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Hemoglobin concentration reflects the blood's oxygen‑carrying capacity. Interpreting low or high values requires understanding physiology, common causes in low‑resource settings, and appropriate investigations.

b: Hb is measured by automated hematology analyzers or manual cyanmethemoglobin method.
Values are influenced by hydration, altitude, and chronic disease.
sections.p: Hemoglobin (Hb) is the iron‑containing protein in red cells that binds oxygen. Concentration is reported in g/dL (g/L in some labs). Normal adult ranges: men 13‑17 g/dL, women 12‑15 g/dL; children vary by age.

b: Anemia severity: mild 10‑12 g/dL, moderate 8‑9.9 g/dL, severe < 8 g/dL.
Polycythemia: Hb > 18 g/dL in men, > 16 g/dL in women.
sections.p: Low Hb (anemia) reduces tissue oxygen delivery; high Hb (polycythemia) increases viscosity and thrombosis risk. Interpretation must consider acute vs chronic, blood loss vs production problems.

b: Anemia contributes to maternal mortality, peri‑operative risk, and poor growth in children.
Polycythemia can be secondary to chronic hypoxia (e.g., COPD, high altitude) or primary (polycythemia vera).
sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals, anemia is a frequent cause of fatigue, dyspnea, and poor surgical outcomes. Polycythemia may present with headache, visual changes, or thrombosis.

t.b: Is the patient anemic or polycythemic? – Low Hb confirms anemia; high Hb confirms polycythemia; also gives MCV, reticulocyte count.
What is the morphology of red cells? – Microcytosis suggests iron deficiency; macrocytosis suggests folate/B12 deficiency; sickle cells point to sickle‑cell disease.
Is iron deficiency present? – Low ferritin confirms iron deficiency anemia; normal/high ferritin with low iron suggests anemia of chronic disease.
Is the marrow responding? – High retics indicate hemolysis or blood loss; low retics suggest production failure.

t.a: HIV test, malaria smear, stool for helminths
t.b: Are infectious causes contributing? – Positive results guide specific therapy.
Is secondary polycythemia due to hypoxia? – Elevated EPO supports secondary cause; normal/low suggests primary.

b: Severe anemia (< 7 g/dL) → urgent blood transfusion if compatible blood available.
Hemolysis (e.g., sickle cell) → folic acid supplementation, infection prophylaxis, consider exchange transfusion in crisis.
Polycythemia vera → low‑dose aspirin, phlebotomy to keep Hb < 16 g/dL; avoid dehydration.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; provide supportive care based on severity.

b: Anemia vs. hypoxia from lung disease – both cause dyspnea but Hb is low only in anemia.
Polycythemia vs. dehydration – dehydration raises Hb transiently; check urine specific gravity.
sections.p: Low Hb vs. low hematocrit (they move together but hematocrit can be falsely low with plasma volume expansion).

b: Chronic disease can cause normal‑range Hb despite iron deficiency (functional iron deficiency).
High altitude raises Hb physiologically; use local reference ranges.
sections.p: Acute blood loss may show normal Hb initially due to hemoconcentration; repeat after fluid resuscitation.

b: Always correlate Hb with clinical signs (pallor, tachycardia, jaundice).
In low‑resource settings, start empiric iron if microcytic anemia and diet low in iron, while awaiting labs.
sections.p: Focus on pattern recognition, severity assessment, and resource‑appropriate work‑up.

whenToSeekHelp: Polycythemia with headache, visual loss, or thrombosis
